question: Which statement best describes Declaring custom properties (--name)?
options: You read a custom property with var(--name). var() accepts an optional fallback used when the property is unset or invalid: var(--accent, #ccc). Fallbacks can even be other var() calls. If a var() resolves to an invalid value for the property, it triggers 'invalid at computed value time' and the property uses its inherited or initial value.

A custom property is any property whose name starts with two dashes, e.g. --brand: #3b82f6. Names are case-sensitive. The value can be almost anything — a color, length, or even a partial token — and it is not validated until used. They are declared inside a normal rule, most often on :root.

Custom properties are inherited by default and participate in the cascade like any property, so specificity and source order decide which declaration wins, and descendants pick up the resolved value. This is why a variable set on a parent automatically flows to children unless re-declared.

Declaring on :root (the html element) makes a variable available globally because custom properties inherit. Declaring on a specific element or class scopes the value to that element and its descendants, overriding the global one locally — the basis of component-level theming.

Sass ($var) variables are compile-time: they are substituted when the stylesheet is built and disappear from the output, so they cannot change at runtime, cascade, or be read by JS. CSS custom properties are runtime, cascading, inheritable, and DOM-aware. Use Sass vars for build-time constants and CSS vars for anything dynamic or themeable.
